opus-5.5.text:
I think contact is really the heart of why manipulation is so hard, and also why it's so interesting. If you look at traditional robotics, a lot of the early successes were in settings where you could avoid contact or treat it very carefully. Think of motion planning for a robot arm in free space: you have rigid-body kinematics and dynamics, and they're smooth and well understood. You can write down the equations, linearize them, and do optimal control. That works beautifully as long as you're not touching anything.

But manipulation is fundamentally about making and breaking contact. The moment the gripper touches an object, or the object touches the table, the dynamics change discretely. You go from free motion to sticking, sliding, rolling, or pushing, and each of those modes has different equations governing it. So the system becomes hybrid: piecewise smooth, with discontinuities at the mode boundaries. That's a nightmare for classical optimization and control, because gradients become uninformative or undefined right where the interesting things happen.

On top of that, the physical quantities that matter, like friction coefficients, surface geometry at the contact patch, and compliance, are very hard to measure and highly sensitive. A tiny change in where you grasp a cup or how much friction there is can completely change the outcome. So even if you have a perfect analytical model in principle, in practice the model is wrong in exactly the places that matter.

The traditional community developed really elegant tools to deal with this: complementarity formulations, contact-implicit trajectory optimization, mode enumeration, quasi-static assumptions for pushing, and so on. I have a lot of respect for that work, and it gives us deep insight into the structure of the problem. But it tends to require very accurate state estimation and object models, and it scales poorly as the number of contacts and objects grows. Think of manipulating a deformable bag or a pile of clothes; the number of possible contact modes just explodes.

So my view is that contact is where the gap between the model and reality is largest, and that's partly why learning-based approaches became so attractive. Instead of explicitly enumerating every contact mode, you can let the system learn, from data, the implicit regularities of how things behave when you touch them. Humans don't solve complementarity problems in their heads when they pick up a mug; we have very good intuitive models built from experience. I don't think that means we should throw away the physics. The structure that traditional methods reveal, like the hybrid nature of contact and the importance of friction cones, can be very valuable as inductive bias. But the question is shifting from "how do we model contact exactly?" to "how do we build systems that can reason about and adapt to contact robustly, even when the model is imperfect?"

r001.rationale: It states that touching an object changes the dynamics discretely, contrasting free motion with contact modes such as sticking, sliding, rolling, or pushing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think contact is really the heart of the problem, and it's also the thing that makes manipulation so much harder than, say, navigation or locomotion in a lot of ways.

If you think about how traditional robotics modeled manipulation, the whole picture was built around rigid-body dynamics. You have a robot arm, you know its kinematics, you know the masses and inertias, and as long as the arm is moving through free space, the dynamics are smooth, differentiable, and basically well understood. You can write down the equations, you can plan trajectories, you can do optimal control. That part of the problem is essentially solved.

The moment the robot touches something, all of that falls apart. Contact introduces discontinuities. The dynamics switch modes the instant two surfaces meet or separate, so you go from a smooth system to a hybrid system with a combinatorial number of possible contact states. Then you add friction, which is notoriously hard to model. Coulomb friction is already a simplification, and real surfaces have stick-slip behavior, deformation, micro-geometry that you can't observe. And then there's the fact that most objects we care about aren't perfectly rigid. A sponge, a cable, a piece of cloth, even a cardboard box all behave in ways that rigid-body assumptions just can't capture.

So in the classical approach, people did tremendous work on things like grasp analysis, form closure and force closure, contact mechanics, and later on contact-implicit trajectory optimization, where you let the optimizer reason about when and where contact happens. Those are beautiful pieces of work. But they all depend on having an accurate model of the object and of the contact interaction, and that's exactly the information you usually don't have in the real world. You don't know the friction coefficient of the cup. You don't know the exact mass distribution. Your perception gives you a noisy point cloud, not a mesh with physical parameters attached.

That's really why I think the field shifted toward learning. Not because the physics is wrong, but because the physics requires parameters you can't reliably obtain, and the errors compound through contact. If your estimate of where the surface is off by a centimeter, in free space that's nothing, but at the moment of contact it's the difference between a successful grasp and knocking the object off the table.

So the way I'd put it is this: contact is where the gap between the model and reality is widest, and it's also where it matters most. The classical view treated it as something to be modeled precisely and planned around. The more modern view, which I find myself in, is that contact is something you have to be robust to, and often the best way to get that robustness is to let the system learn from experience and from feedback, rather than trying to predict everything from first principles ahead of time.

r001.rationale: The response says that before contact the dynamics are smooth and well understood, while contact causes mode switches and turns the system into a hybrid one.

astra-6.text:
I think contact is really central to manipulation. When a robot moves through free space, its dynamics are relatively straightforward to model. But as soon as it touches an object, you have to account for the interaction: where the contact happens, how much force is applied, whether the surfaces stick or slide, and how friction affects the motion.

Traditionally, we model this using different contact modes—no contact, sticking, sliding—and the transitions between them. Within a particular mode, you can often write down a reasonable dynamics model. The difficult part is that a small change in motion can cause the contact mode to switch, and suddenly the object behaves differently. So contact is both what allows the robot to manipulate the world and what makes modeling and planning for manipulation challenging.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts relatively straightforward free-space dynamics with the interaction dynamics required once the robot touches an object, communicating a fundamental change after contact begins.

sol-6.1.text:
Contact is really central to manipulation, because it’s how a robot applies forces to an object and changes its motion. But it’s also what makes the dynamics difficult to model. Before contact, the robot and the object can move independently. Once they touch, their motions become coupled, and what happens depends on where the contact occurs, friction, and whether the surfaces are sticking or sliding.

In traditional approaches, we often represent those as distinct contact modes, each with its own equations and constraints. The challenge is predicting when the system switches between them. Even a small error in the object’s position can mean the robot makes contact earlier or later than expected, which can produce a very different outcome. So the difficulty isn’t just modeling motion within a contact mode; it’s handling those transitions reliably.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts independent motion before contact with coupled motion once the robot and object touch, clearly stating that contact changes the manipulation dynamics.
